That the Speaker do not now leave the chair, but that it be resolved that this House, because of the failure of the government to implement promises contained in the Speech from the Throne, and for other causes, has no longer any confidence in the present government.
He said:	At the opening of parliament we
were presented with a Speech from the Throne forecasting certain legislation which was to be introduced in this House. The Speech from the Throne states that legislation will be enacted under which the natural resources of the province of Alberta will be restored to that province, and in an answer to a question I addressed to the Prime Minister yesterday we were assured that the government has no intention during this session of carrying out the promises it made in that Speech from the Throne. Following the Speech from the Throne an agreement was entered into between the government of Alberta and the government of the Dominion of Canada, which agreement was signed by ministers representing both governments. I submit that that agreement should be lived up to. If we flout the will of parliament and deceive the people we sacrifice that prestige parliament should enjoy in the estimation of the country. That is my reason for this motion. Having been a member of the legislature of Alberta, I in common with the present Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) and other members on the government side of the House, placed myself on record as favouring the restoration of the natural resources of Alberta to that province and with them supported a memorial to that effect addressed to this parliament. Now that that question is before the House I hope each member will give consideration, not merely to the question of the restoration of the resources to the province, but also to that of the fulfilment of the promise this government made to the government of Alberta. Upon that one question I desire through the medium of this motion to place every member of the House on record.

I offer no apology to the House for having my name coupled with that of the hon. member for East Calgary in introducing this motion. We have been in session since the 7th of January, and up to the present time, looking over the record of this government, what do we find? I submit that we can find very little, practically nothing, in the way of legislation. There is only one thing I desire to say in seconding the motion, and that is in connection with the matter of the appointment of the royal commission to invest'gate Maritime rights or the wrongs of the Maritimes? I will not say anything whatever about the personnel of

The government has appointed as secretaries of that commission two gentlemen in the province of Nova Scotia, who are worthy, estimable and good citizens in every way, but who took such a stand against the Maritimes and what we call Maritime rights during the last campaign that I submit, Sir, their minds are too prejudiced in the matter and that they should not be appointed or permitted to	take	part in	the deliberations of	thatcommission. I submit if one secretary is to be	selected from	amongst those who wereoutstanding in criticism or opposition to Maritime rights the other appointee should be	one	who is	sympathetic towards	thematter.	I claim	it is unfair to have	two
gentlemen of the same political stripe on that commission.
Mr. T L. CHURCH (Toronto Northwest): In referring to the return of the natural resources of the province of Alberta, 4 wish to say that the Minister of the Interior, on the 18th March last, placed on the order paper a resolution approving the agreement made between the Dominion of Canada and the government of Alberta respecting the transfer of public lands in the province of Alberta.
The government made this announcement in the Speech from the Throne:
Your attention will be invited, among other measures, to a bill to provide for the transfer to the province of Alberta of its natural resources.
On the 18th March a resolution was placed on the order paper by the Minister of the Interior to bring about this legislation. It practically has been dropped as the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice and the Minister of the Interior announced in the House. The Prime Minister only yesterday repeated the statement.

I rise to a
point of order. My point is that the subject matter of the resolution standing on the order paper in regard to the agreement made between the Dominion government and the Alberta government cannot be debated now under this resolution.

I wish to point out, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister announced some time ago that the government were not going to go on with this resolution to which the hon. gentleman now refers. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) said the same thing
{Mr. Quinn.]
a month ago. The point is not well taken for May at page 249 says with regard to anticipation:
In determining however, whether a discussion is out of order on the ground of anticipation, the Speaker must have regard to the probability of the matter anticipated being brought before the House within a reasonable time.
I am not discussing the motion on the order paper. I am supporting the amendment now before the House and not touching the text of the resolution referred to.

I
submit that the point of order is not well taken. We are not discussing one way or the other the merits of the resolution now standing on the order paper; we are discussing the failure of the government to implement its pledges, its promises. It would be a most extraordinary thing if a vote of lack of confidence on such grounds could not be moved simply because the government keeps on the order paper an order which it has no intention of going on with and the merits of which are not challenged in the present discussion.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Perhaps I would not have raised the point of order personally, but as regards the discussion of the matter I think the point is well taken. I would refer Your Honour to Beauchesne at page 38, section 146, under rule 13 relating to discussions taking place before going into supply or on motions that are moved before going into supply. This section concludes:
Provided that the discussion and the amendment-
The discussion as well as the amendment.
-if one is moved, shall not relate to any decision of the House during the current session, nor to any item of the estimates, nor to any resolution to be proposed to the committee of Ways and Means, nor to any matter placed on or whereof notice has been given in the order paper.
Therefore no discussion can be allowed before going into supply when it relates-that is the language-to a matter placed on or whereof notice has been given in the order paper. The discussion which the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) has started relates to a matter which is on the order paper.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I have very few words to say on the point of order. The point of order must go merely to the matter of the discussion and not to the matter of the

Want oj Confidence Motion
amendment itself. It is too manifest for debate that the amendment itself is in order. As to the discussion, it may be under the portion quoted by the Minister of Justice that the merits or demerits of a motion now on the order paper cannot be reviewed. I do not think the speaker though has got so far as to discuss the merits or demerits of the motion and consequently he would be in order. But is it not most extraordinary that the government, having abandoned a motion by official and specific renunciation in this House, can by retention of that motion obstinately and worthlessly on the order paper effectively shut out from the discussion of this assembly any matter related to it? I am indeed surprised that the government would suggest that they could be justified in taking such a course. If they are sincerely of the view that while they retain this on the order paper after having renounced it in this House as any portion of government policy it does interfere with discussion, clearly it would be their duty immediately to ask for its removal from the order paper.

Does any other hon. member desire to speak on the point of order? I will now give my ruling. I read in Beauchesne page 38, No. 146:
Whenever an order of the day has been read for the House to resolve itself into the committee of Supply or the committee of Ways and Means, the motion "That the Speaker do now leave the chair" must be proposed, except in cases provided by rule 17c. When such motion is proposed, it shall be permissible to discuss any public matter within the powers of the federal parliament or to ask for the redress of any grievance, and it is not necessary to move an amendment for that purpose; provided that the discussion and the amendment, if one is moved, shall not relate to any decision of the House during the current session, nor to any item of the estimates, nor to any resolution to be proposed to the committee of Ways and Means, nor to any matter placed on or whereof notice has been given in the order paper.
This is based upon Bourinot, May, Red-lich and Bourke. In the present instance a motion has been moved that I do now leave the chair for the House to resolve itself into committee of Supply. To that motion an amendment is moved expressing the view that the government, not having implemented its promises, has lost the confidence of the House. I give the amendment in general terms. The amendment itself is drafted according to the rules and it is in order. But the discussion as stated in Beauchesne, according to Bourinot, May, Redlich and Bourke, must not bear on questions which are still standing on the order paper. The hon. member for Joliette has mentioned that there stands on the order paper in the name of the government a
resolution dealing with the return to Alberta of its natural resources. That is the point at issue. Can any hon. member, upon an amendment or a motion which is itself in order, discuss a question standing on the order paper? On that point I may quote from May at page 248:
A motion must not anticipate a matter already appointed for consideration by the House, whether it be a bill or an adjourned debate upon a motion. A motion is equally out of order, if it anticipates a notice of motion for leave to bring in a bill that includes a subject proposed to be dealt with by the motion. A matter already appointed for consideration by the House cannot be anticipated by an amendment, while a notice of motion as long as it remains upon the paper, whether for a specified day or not, prevents its subject-matter being discussed by means of an amendment to a motion or of a motion for the adjournment of the House, including a motion under standing order No. 10.
The same view is held by Bourinot, at page 320:
An amendment cannot anticipate a notice of mot on on the order paper.
It is true, as I have ruled, that the motion in amendment presented by the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Davis) is properly drafted and in order; it is broad in its terms. But discussion upon that amendment must bear on the subject and must not impinge upon nor anticipate a question already appointed for consideration by the House.
I find in Denison's and Brand's Decisions on this point several instances confirming the view I have advanced. For example, at page 118, under the caption "Anticipating Discussion," the following decision is given:
Mr. Speaker said it was out of order to discuss amendments to a bill which would come before the House at a subsequent period of the evening. ... In a debate on the arrangement of public business, it is not in order to discuss a bill w'hich is to come on at a later period.
At page 119 this decision is given by Brand:
It is irregular to discuss a motion on the paper for a future day.
The question in this instance had reference to the treaty of Washington, and it bears an analogy to the present one. According to Brand:
An hon. member having placed a notice on the paper cannot, while another subject is before the House, refer to the subject of that motion, even under the plea of illustration.
Brand again, at page 119:
When a bill is before the House it is not competent, by a motion on the same subject, to anticipate discussion.

TFanf uj Confidence Motion
Denison goes still further:
When the further consideration of a bill is postponed it is not in order, by moving a resolution in the interval, to raise the whole question.
I rule, therefore, that while the proposed amendment is perfectly in order the discussion thereupon must be confined entirely to the subject of that amendment and must not embrace any question which is already on the order paper.
Mr. CHURC'H:	I accept your ruling on
the point of order, Mr. Speaker, and I have no wish in view thereof to discuss the amendment further, as I hope to have an opportunity later on of dealing with the whole Alberta resources question. However, I wish to point out that Sir Erskine May at page 249, twelfth edition, qualifies the rule respecting anticipation as follows:
In determining, however, whether the discussion is out of order on the ground of anticipation, the speaker must have regard to the probability of the matter anticipated being brought before the House within a reasonable time.
The Speech from the Throne contains this definite statement of government policy:
Your attention will be invited, among other measures, to a bill to provide for the transfer to the province of Alberta of its natural resources, and to a bill amending the Dominion Elections Act.
This promise, although not carried out, was followed on March 18 by a resolution, still on the order paper, to turn the resources over to the province. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Edmonton) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) both intimated that this resolution would not be gone on with, and so did the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) in making his statement of policy on the orders of the day to refer the validity of the Alberta Act, 1905, and of section 17 particularly, to the Supreme Court, notwithstanding that its validity has never been questioned. The Prime Minister yesterday on the orders of the day, in answer to the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Davis), stated that it was not the intention of the government to make this transfer at the present session. There 'can therefore be no question of anticipation under these circumstances. Alberta should get her resources free of all conditions whatever.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Before I discuss the
amendment, may I direct the attention of the House to the circumstance that this is

the first notification which the government has had of any intention on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite to move a motion of this kind. It is a courtesy of long established usage and precedent that when a motion, in the nature of a want of confidence motion, is to be directed against the government, the leader of the opposition or some of his party notifies the ministry in advance of such intention. Hon. gentlemen opposite have not seen fit to follow this practice on the present occasion, and inasmuch as they must undoubtedly be aware of the custom, I can conceive of only one reason for the course they have adopted, that is the hope that by springing a motion of this kind suddenly, when all their members are present while some on the opposite side are possibly absent, they may be able to score against the administration. If that is the motive of my hon. friends, the sooner they score the better. If this administration does not enjoy the confidence of the House of Commons, the sooner we know it the better, and we will carry our appeal from parliament to the country.
This motion in its language is as general as any motion can possibly be made. It specifies nothing in particular, it simply alleges that the government because of failure to implement promises contained in the Speech from the Throne, and for other reasons which are not specified, has no longer the confidence of the House. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that we have not yet reached the conclusion of this session and that it is therefore impossible for the members of the House to say whether or not the government will implement the various promises contained in the Speech from the Throne. No one can make such an assertion until the last word has been heard in this House with respect to the several measures which have been mentioned in the Speech. If hon. members will read the Speech from the Throne they will, I think, be agreeably surprised to discover to what extent the government has carried out the promises therein made. I will make this statement without fear of contradiction, that never since this parliament has been in existence has it been possible, owing to one circumstance or another, for governments to fulfil all the undertakings they have set forth in speeches from the throne. The session is entered upon with every intention on the part of a government to carry out its entire programme as outlined in the Speech, but

Want oj Confidence Motion
until the government, as the session proceeds, discovers what may be possible, it is not in a position to make any final statement with respect to every item in the forecast.
One item has been mentioned, and only one, in regard to which the government apparently, according to hon. gentlemen opposite, is not about to make good its undertaking.. That is the item which appears as follows in the Speech from the Throne:
Your attention will be invited, among other measures, to a 'bill to provide for the transfer to the province of Alberta of its natural resources.
If I wished to take that language literally I could submit to this House that it has been fulfilled-the attention of the House has been invited to the measure.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am not saying that I wish to take it literally; I do not intend to, but if I did I could point to the fact that the attention of the House has been invited to that measure. However, when that language was put in the Speech from the Throne-

Order. I would remind
the right hon. gentleman I have just ruled that it is out of order to discuss the merits or demerits of the resolution he is referring o.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I have no desire to discuss the question of the transfer of its natural resources to Alberta. But I would ask your ruling as to whether or not I would be justified in informing the House why that particular measure is not being proceeded with at the present time.
Order.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is the
only point I should like to know whether I am free to speak on.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MBTGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may
be permitted, I would support the Prime Minister's contention in every particular. I surely feel he has an absolute right to speak on that restricted point. *

According to all the
authorities I have quoted, it is not permissible to discuss the merits or demerits of a question which is already on the order paper. Of course, if both sides agree that the right hon.
gentleman may discuss the particular feature of the question mentioned by him, it is .permissible.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
if there is any objection, as there appears to be to my making any mention of that particular point I shall refrain from so doing I have no desire to go beyond the rules in the slightest degree. However, hon. gentlemen will be able to conclude for themselves the reasons that have caused the government to indicate the course with respect to this particular measure that has seemed advisable to it.
Now. if one looks at the Speech from the Throne, the outstanding undertaking is that the government hoped in the course of this session as a result of its past policies and its present measures to be able to afford substantial relief to the taxpayers of this country, that it hoped to be able to lower the customs tariff on commodities that arc in general use by the people and that it hoped to reduce taxation in other ways. The House knows that after very considerable discussion in this chamber the government has succeeded in reducing the duty on automobiles by 15 per cent.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But we have.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not wonder that hon. gentlemen opposite groan; that is where the shoe pinches. What the people of this country are interested in at the present time is a reduction of taxation, and that has been the great objective of this government. Session after session we have made reductions, and this session we have made possibly the greatest measure of reduction in taxation that has ever been made in any session of parliament. On automobiles of $1,200 value and under we have reduced the customs duties by 15 per cent. In addition to that, with respect to automobiles of that value manufactured in this country, we have removed the war tax of 5 per cent, giving consumers the corresponding benefit. We have removed the taxation which wns put on receipts, a form of taxation which had come to present many difficulties to retailers throughout Canada, and which meant an additional burden to the people themselves. There has been a reduction in the income tax all along the line. Besides that we have removed taxation in other forms; for instance we have undertaken to say that on July 1

Want oj Confidence Motion
this year we will return to penny postage in the Dominion, and we intend to see that that promise is implemented. I might mention other things in the same category, in all of which the people are most vitally interested; but I will not take up the time of the House in going over the record of the administration in that regard.
I should like to draw the attention of the House to one remark made in the course of this debate, namely, that a great deal of time has been spent this session and verjr little accomplished. May I ask, who was responsible for the time that has been consumed? Hon. gentlemen opposite spent nearly a month at the beginning of the session discussing whether or not the present administration was to be permitted to carry on.

Your party did just as
much discussing as ours.
Some hon. MEMBERS; Order.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In the course of the discussion on the tariff, another debate lasting a month, more or less, took place, for which hon. gentlemen opposite, I think, ought to share the main measure of responsibility.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that to carry on government this session has not been an easy matter for the administration,-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
-but I do
say that no other party or group in this parliament could have carried on at all. I think the administration deserves the greater credit in that, under circumstances such as we have been confronted with, we have been able to carry on so successfully, and to give to the country the benefit of so much useful legislation.
May I repeat in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that this motion prefers no specific charge against the government in any way; it is a general want of confidence motion. It means, of course, that if this motion carries the government will have to consider the next step to be taken.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Let me tell
hon. gentlemen opposite at once the step that will be taken. If this government does not enjoy the confidence of the House it will lose no time in asking for a dissolution of parliament and making its appeal from the House to the country.
FMr. Mackenzie King.]

Mr. Speaker, it had been my intention not to let parliament close without making a protest against certain promises contained in the Speech from the Throne not having been carried out, and it was only due to the fact that I was endeavouring with some of my colleagues to draft a resolution to-day that would not be challenged on the ground that it dealt with a resolution now on the order paper that I was not in my seat this afternoon to raise this question myself.
Now, every hon. member is well acquainted with the situation we faced at the beginning of the session. At that time I did not see eye to eye with the majority of my colleagues as to the party that should be called upon to form the government. However, I was overruled. I then stated to them that I was down here to get certain legislation, and so long as the government would implement the pledges contained in the Speech from the Throne I was prepared to stand behind and assist it to carry on. Had the government done so, I would still consider it my duty to stand behind it. However, one of the questions that vitally affects the people of Alberta, a question in which they are all keenly interested, whether they be Liberal, Conservative or Progressive, is the return of the natural resources to their province. We have discussed this matter with the government, and some few days ago, I think it was on June 2, the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) made a statement to the House. On the day following I asked the government if they would not reconsider their position and bring in a measure to transfer the natural resources to the province of Alberta. The answer is on Hansard.
We have not taken the government by surprise in this matter. We have discussed it with them very freely. We did so yesterday, and we were told that nothing was going to be done this session, and therefore, Mr. Speaker, so far as I am concerned, while I have felt that I was in duty bound to support the government so long as they were willing to do their part, now that they have failed so far as Alberta is concerned in that one question that is vital to us, I feel that I am relieved from that responsibility, and I shall have to take my own course. I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that if it had not been for a signed agreement, an agreement which was signed on January 9, this government wTould never have been in power to start with.

speechtext: My hon. friend has referred to some signed agreement. I do not know to what he is referring.

Ernest Lapointe and the Hon. Charles Stewart, for the Dominion of Canada, and by the Hon. J. E. Brownlee and the Hon. Vernon W. Smith, for the province of Alberta. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not know whether my hon. friend is in order in alluding to the natural resources, but if he is permitted to do so, and is going to read one agreement, I would ask him to read also the supplementary agreement which sets forth the exact terms of the bills which were to be brought into both Houses.
In view of the authorities cited and having regard to parliamentary jurisprudence, I cannot allow the agreement to be read. I assume it refers to the natural resources.

It was not my intention to
read this agreement. Mr. Speaker, but the Prime Minister asked me to what agreement 1 referred and naturally I had to state what it was.
I do not know that there is any need of going into a long discussion of this matter, but the hon. members from Alberta feel that they cannot go home to their people without having found a satisfactory solution for it. While I would prefer to have brought in a resolution which would have dealt specifically with this question, seeing that it is already on the order paper and cannot be discussed, a vote of want of confidence is the only way in which the matter can be dealt with, and I am therefore prepared to support the resolution.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no matter what colour my hon. friends opposite may place on their resolution introduced to-day to show that they at least have no confidence in the government, the government realize full well what is behind the resolution. From the day parliament met until this very hour, even up until yesterday, the question discussed most in this House was not a question of any particular item mentioned in the Speech from the
Throne, but a question as between high tariff and low tariff. That was the question that was brought forcibly before the 3 p.m. country by hon. gentlemen who lead the opposition, and it was upon the question of high tariff or low tariff that they challenged our right as a government to carry on. We gave them our answer on the 15th of April when we brought down the budget, when we reduced the duty on automobiles, when we made reductions all along the line in the income tax, when we removed altogether the receipt tax, when we removed the ^sales tax from certain items in which the people of this country were most interested, and when we announced that on the 1st of July we would restore penny postage. Hon. gentlemen opposite may challenge the government's right to carry on, but I submit that the country is not going to be fooled by this resolution presented to-day. We are prepared as a government to have this question settled once and for all, and the sooner we have the vote and the sooner we know whether the policy of high and higher and still higher tariffs is going to prevail in this country, or the policy of the government, which is a policy that has led to the encouragement of our trade all over the world, the better it will be for Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. M. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a very
peculiar situation is before the House. My hon. friend from East Calgary (Mr. Davis) w has moved a resolution of a very general character and in the course of his address he stated that the ground of his moving it was one subject, and one subject only. Your Honour has ruled that that subject cannot be a matter of discussion in this debate, so that so far as this resolution is concerned, according to your ruling, Mr. Speaker, the matter referred to by the hon. member for East Calgary is eliminated from consideration by this House in this debate.
Oh.

My
hon. friends intimate that I am not correct. Let me say this: If the Speaker's ruling is right, then the one, and only one, question that my hon. friend from East Calgary siid he wanted to submit is not before the House at this time.
The only other matter that has been suggested as a reason why this government has lost the confidence of the country was supplied by the junior member for Halifax (Mr Quinn), who, while admitting that the government had carried out the promise contained

I accept the apology in the spirit in which it is intended. Now, Mr. Speaker, the amendment declares further that there are other causes why this House should vote want of confidence in the government, but the time taken would be too considerable if I were to undertake to review that phase of the motion. Those other causes are so numerous that little can be gained by discussing them at this time. I will, however, emphasize one of them, and about two sentences will end what I have to say. This government cannot enjoy the confidence of the country while it fails to present to parliament any definite policy upon any subject whatever. It is a government by compromise, a government by intrigue. This government sits in office because of intrigue. The government sits in office because of pretences, of promises made which it never intended to carry through. It sits in office because of solemn pledges made and repeated and embalmed in the most sacred form, which today it ruthlessly repudiates.
The Prime Minister says, "If this vote goes against us you men are going to have to go back to your constituencies and fight an election". There is the sword held over hon. members of this House. May I remind the Prime Minister that the question of dissolution is not one within his prerogative to decide. There is no region in the whole realm of autocracy into which the right hon. gentleman is not prepared to soar, if by so doing he can hold office for another week or another day. But there are regions into which he cannot enter, into which he is forbidden. This government conducted the last election campaign under its own auspices; it appointed its own officials. And, hon. gentlemen, I have heard one of them especially, his eye glancing in the direction of Peace River-declare	that
"Liberalism" is now more alive than ever. The result of the government's control of the election machinery is now public and open before the electors of Canada, and these Ministers should hesitate ever to ask to be placed in charge of election machinery again. But even if they do, this parliament was elected on the government's appeal; this parliament was elected under the auspices of this government, and if the government is not able to carry through its policy, is not able to retain the confidence of a parliament so elected, then its duty is to resign. That is the only right this government has. The Prime Minister knows this full well, but he believes that the threat of dissolution may be effective in turning one or two votes in a division. The threat of dissolution is launched only for the purpose of frightening those whom the Prims 
Minister believes to be timid and susceptible to such a threat. But, I repeat, neither the prerogative nor the right of dissolution is his. There are however open to him both a right and a duty, and these he can embrace only by the act of resignation, for he- must know that he has not the confidence either of this parliament or of the people of Canada.

I have only now had an opportunity of looking at the amendment which has been proposed, for when I asked foir it a little while ago it was in circulation right and left. Evidently it is of much interest. I have heard the -comment of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen). and there is a good deal of truth in what the right hon. gentleman has said. As a matter of fact, if one w-e-re to take the history of parliament, session after session, ever since confederation, pretty much the same comment might be made upon the course of governments. I have sat in this House for eleven years, and have read to a considerable extent the records of parliament both before and since that period, and I cannot recall one single session in which the entire programme as announced in the Speech from the Throne has been fulfilled either by Conservative or by Liberal administrations. In that respect I make bold to say, at the risk of scandalizing some -of the virginal minds opposite, that I do not feel quite so exercised over the failure of the government to implement every paragraph of the Speech from the Throne by a specific piece of legislation. It is. I think, a mistake to put too much into speeches from the throne; it would be preferable to announce less and to accomplish more. This however has been the habit of governments; and I do not fancy that any member of this House who decided to support the present admin:stra-tion in preference to one formed from the Conservative party-because that was the only alternative-would be justified -in voting for this resolution for the reasons that have been advanced this afternodn and those that are contained in the resolution itself. Of course there is the qualifying -phrase "and for other causes", which is very broad. There may be many causes or reasons for voting confidence or want of confidence in a government. therefore put to hon. gentlemen the question I ask myself: Has anything occurred during this session which would warrant those of us who have elected to support this government rather than a Conservative government, led and inspired by the right hon. gentleman opposite (Mr. Meighen), and holding the principles which the party' opposite holds, has

anything occurred to justify us in changing our attitude, in departing from the course we have followed for five months, and throwing down the government in office in order to gave their opponents an opportunity 'to take their place? Because that after all is the question.
Now, many situations connected with parliamentary government are illogical. Very often one is forced to choose between supporting a government in which he is not oveT-confident and putting into its place an opposition in which he has no confidence at all. or decidedly less confidence. To my mind this is the situation that presents itself to those of us who, not having been elected as members of the Liberal party and blind supporters of the Liberal government, have now to take their stand courageously and make their choice between the policies presented by the Liberal government and the policies presented by the Conservative party. There is no other choice. By supporting a resolution of this kind we cannot create a new party that will satisfy all we ask for. Even if he assumed power as the result of a snap vote or of an election waged under the same conditions as obtained in 1917, when ballot boxes were stuffed in the pretence of saving the empire, although damning the morals of the country, the right hon. gentleman's usefulness would be impaired so long as he and some 
men of broad mind and strong hand in his party failed to crush the eggs that are being hatched in the nest of traitors season after season.
Now I have gone beyond the letter of the motion, but I think iit was just as well. If this amendment is to be the preface to an appeal to the people of Canada it is well that a few men, who are absolutely free to say what they think of one party or the other, should stand up here and speak in the name of those numerous Canadians in Quebec and in Ontario, in the east and in the west, who are thinking less from day to day from the narrow point of view of party and more and more from the standpoint of a true national policy for this country. Whether one party or the other does the right thing is utterly immaterial to me. Suppose we had an election and came back to the House, as is likely, and found ourselves in a situation similar to that which faced us at the opening of this session. Suppose hon. gentlemen opposite had the advantage of numbers to start with; suppose they formed a government. I think I voice the feeling of those men and women who have given me their confidence not only in the small portion of Quebec which I represent but throughout the province, the men and women who rightly or wrongly have chosen me as their mouthpiece for some years past, as well as the feeling of a growing number of English-speaking Protestants in Ontario, in eastern and in western Canada, when I say that the government which under such circumstances would command the respect of the people would be not one which would attempt to secure a victory by means of a snap vote, but one which would consult the interests of the country at large. Let us who speak independently for the people admit that we are a very small body of men; but I venture to say that the party which will win and retain the enduring confidence of the people of Canada will be that party which will espouse a policy the most Canadian and the most national in military matters, in foreign affairs, in economics and in relations between race and race whether within or outside of Canada. It will be the party which will do the most to re-establish, as the basis of government, equal rights as between the various sections of the country and mutual respect as between east and west and as between French and English. This end will not be attained by any attempt to take advantage of the first opportunity to rouse the Orange lodges against the hierarchy or to enrage Quebec at the expense of Alberta. It will not be done that way. It will be done

Want of Confidence Motion
by a constant effort upon the best minds in all the provinces and in all parties to look for the broader, for the bigger, for the most solid and enduring policy. If we do that we will find that we have turned a long circle and come back to what was once the standard policy of the Conservative party, the policy which enabled the alliance of Macdonald and Cartier- not upon any small calculation as to the misdoing of their Liberal opponents in this little matter or that little matter, not upon the advantage that could be gained by getting the support of the bishops in the province of Quebec and of George Brown and his clear Grits in his appeals against Romanism in the province of Ontario. No, it did better than that. Macdonald and Cartier took the leader of those men, George Brown, in their government; *-I admit they did not keep him long, but they kept him long enough to muzzle him while confederation was consummated, to prevent him from introducing in the new-born nations the poison which he had been distilling for so many years in Upper Canada. The result endured for some time; but unfortunately, the venom had not disappeared. It started again in Ontario, it extended to the west, and it was taken up by some Liberals and by some Conservatives.
What did it achieve? What has been the result to Canada as a whole, morally, socially or politically, of every encroachment made by any government, Conservative or Liberal, upon the principle of minority rights? What has been gained to Canada by any abandonment of the sound national policy with regard to participation in imperial affairs? What has been gained, I ask? More prejudice to-day as between French and English than there was fifty years ago; more cleavage as between Catholic and Protestant than there was fifty years ago-less violent, I admit, but perhaps more subtle. That is in regard to inter-racial matters in Canada. With regard to outside affairs there is to-day less unity in matters of national import. Why? Because we have appealed alternately to the British to think of Britain first and of Canada second; and to French Canadians to enlist and fight for France instead of remaining here and working for Canada. Thereby we have revived the old colonial, racial spirit in every group in Canada.
But the reaction is on, and I am happy to say it is perhaps to-day stronger in English Canada than in French Canada. I venture to predict that the party that will win the heart even of British Canada within the next ten years will be the party that will unfurl, not the Union Jack-the Union Jack will be
respected so long as the present system continues, so long as we remain in a free alliance with Great Britain-but the flag of Canada, the party that will put itself courageously, frankly and intelligently at the head of the nationalistic instincts of the people of Canada east and west, English and French. I know this looks venturesome, I know this may be considered as the back thought of an old eccentric; but that old eccentric has kept some of the youth of heart and mind in him, has remained in contact with both old and young Canadians in all parts of Canada, and he receives daily communications from people in Canada born in the Old Country. Let me take this only as an example. One English-born Canadian told me, not long ago: You express our feelings, but we are yet too much under the domination of racial pride and the prejudice of tradition to admit it; but go on speak your mind-which is ours- and the time is coming when our sons, who will be one degree more Canadian than we are, will go in advance of you because you will be too British for them. I a*m beginning to find that out.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in this long-I will not call it oration-rambling, if you like, I have given time to gentlemen on all sides of the House to make due reflection. I noticed when I began to speak there was some excitement; now some hon. gentlemen are on the point of sleeping, which is a good cure for nervousness. At any rate, they have had time for reflection, which is a good thing for the mind, and therefore I hope when we come to vote on this amendment it will be in one of two ways. If judged within the narrow circle of its wording, well, it will be treated as all similar motions have been treated this session; it is the same thing in different words. If, on the contrary, it is taken in a broad way, I for one am prepared to thank the right hon. gentleman for having enlarged the scope of the motion, for having talked outside it and made perhaps what he expects to be his first electoral speech, in which event I think we should follow him on that ground. But then, this motion is not worded in such terms as to inspire those thoughts or reflections that will enable any member of this House or any ordinary elector to see that it leads to anything. It is no declaration of principle on the part of the Conservative party. It is such a vague denunciation of the attitude of the Liberal government that really no Conservative can find much solace in it; and I do not think Liberals can be much exercised over it, except perhaps if they are short of a sufficient
Want oj Confidence Motion

number of votes to give them a majority, which from a certain point of view is absolutely immaterial to me. But surely it is not upon a motion of this nature that a great party, boasting its historic traditions, lays all its future hopes of success. But perhaps that should raise my hopes, for it shows there is more conscience in the Conservative party than I gave them credit for; they feel they are so far away from their great traditions that they must not express them, they must minimize their policy in as few words as possible, and in words that carry as little significance as possible. I think that is a form of sincerity which is to be commended. It proves that they are in the process of evolution. Perhaps within a session or two, or after a couple of elections, they will have found their way to Damascus, they will have seen some of the true light. It may blind them at first, but after the cure has operated-of course if they have grace enough to be worthy of cure -they will see things through the new medium and will change their tactics. I do not mean their board1 of strategy. I do not know the gentlemen composing that board, but I am quite sure there must be in it men who do not see things exactly as some others do, there must be some few differences in aspirations, in ideals and even in polities. I am quite sure of it. I should not like to calumniate the gentlemen opposite with such stupidity as to imagine that nine or ten of them could always agree upon everything. There must be a tendency upwards and downwards. I think unfortunately I am expressing the view of a large number of people outside the House when I say that the tendency downwards has manifested itself quite often during the session. We have heard heroics about the great principles of economics all connected, as I have said before, with the four wheels of a motor car. We have heard tremendous denunciations, but, after all, what has it come to? To a few motions of nonconfidence, very unhappily worded. In fact, it looked at times, and I said so at the beginning of the session, as if the government had to thank the Conservative board of strategy, for it has certainly saved this government on more than one occasion, and it ought to be as successful this time as it has been on previous occasions. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I need not say that I would not think for one moment of supporting this motion. I am sorry the session should end with such a poor, meagre, expression of opinion on the part of the great Conservative party, previous to what they expect to be an appeal to the people either this year or 
next. I think it behooves them and would be to the advantage of the country if the Conservative party would decide at last to frame a great policy in clear-cut words that would really express something to the minds of the people who are thirsting for ideas and principles, much less for words and for tactics.

Mr. Speaker, coming from t'he province of Alberta and' being deeply interested in this question, I feel that in my feeble way I should like to say a few words. Being but * a child in parliamentary life and experience I feel that it is a high honour to be permitted to follow one so experienced and so eloquent as the hon. member for La'belle (Mr. Bourassa), who has just sat down. While I am compelled to admire his power in debate and the many admirable qualities which he possesses, I regret to say, Mr. Speaker, that I cannot see eye to eye with him on the matter that is now before the House.
He has mentioned the word " party " a number of times in his address, I think perhaps with a degree of nervousness. We have been told time and again in this House that principles are greater than party, and I claim, Mr. Speaker, that a principle is involved here which is greater than any party. The hon. member for Laibelle has also shown a great desire for Canadian unity. With that I am in full accord, because I claim there is no member of this House who has a greater desire for Canadian unity than myself. Like the hon. member for Labelle I can also claim to be a Canadian. The blood of four or five generations of forebears runs through my veins. When my ancestors came to Nova Scotia in the year 1753 that province was wooded right down to the shore 5 p.m. line, and those men had to go into the forests and hew out a place in order to provide themselves with humble homesteads. I have lived in the province of Nova Scotia half of my lifetime. The other half I have lived in the province of Alberta, that great province which in a few years will hold its millions of people, and in which I am proud to represent the important district of Vegreville at the present time in this House. I say I am very anxious for Canadian unity. I hold up my hands, while living in that province, to the province of British Columbia on the west, to the prairie provinces, to the central provinces, and to the Martime provinces down by the sea. I want to see them all bound together in one spirit of national unity that will be conducive to the prosperity of this great Dominion of ours.

Want of Confidence Motion
Reference has been made to a certain agreement. When the executive of this group called upon the Prime Minister in the early days of this session, I was given to understand that that agreement was signed, and the signing of that agreement, as stated by the hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Lucas), had considerable influence in directing the minds of the members from the province of Alberta. Not only did I understand that that agreement was signed, but I was shown the pen which was used at the time the agreement was signed. When the announcement was made on January 22 or 23-I forget the exact date-at a large farmers' convention at Calgary, that Alberta was going to get her natural resources, it evoked a great deal of enthusiasm and deep satisfaction, and when later the Prime Minister rose in his place and made the distinct announcement that a certain measure by which Alberta would get her natural resources would not be proceeded with at this session, I was greatly disappointed, and I felt that any agreement or any responsibility that I had in regard to supporting the government ceased from that moment. The pledge given, as I considered it to be at that time, was deliberately broken. That is the way I felt about it. I do not intend to detain the House any longer, because hon gentlemen know my mind. I rose merely to place myself in full accord with all those sentiments that have been so ably expressed by my hon. friend from Camrose.. In regard to the action of the Prime Minister, let me say that if I voted against this amendment I should be saying to the people of Alberta that I approved of his action. That Mr Speaker, I cannot do.

Mr. Speaker, with the subject matter of the amendment I have no quarrel and could have none. One who is aligned with or supporting any political party is bound to meet with opposition from the opposing party. It has always been so, and I presume always will be so. But notwithstanding the fact that we may divide into groups, there will always be but two sides to any question, and we will find ourselves aligned on the one side or the other. I have no exception to take to the motion of my hon. friend from East Calgary (Mr. Davis). He may at any time test the feeling of this House with respect to the confidence that may be reposed in the government. The mover of this amendment did not embody in it its real purpose. That is evident because immediately after moving the amendment he took the opportunity of stating the grounds upon which
is was based. The amendment simply alleges that the government has not implemented its pledges as announced in the Speech from the Throne. Well, Mr. Speaker, we have listened to the leader of the opposition, who spoke for the party responsible for the amendment, and save in one particular he has not been able to find any particular fault with the actions of the government in regard to the legislation introduced at the present session. The one shortcoming of which he complained is that we have not introduced, up to the present, legislation for the amendment of the Election Act. Stripping all verbiage from the speech of my right hon. friend, that is the sole particular as to which he makes complaint, with one exception, and I will deal it in a moment. That is the only respect in which he finds fault with the government and charges it with being recreant to its pledges. The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) has made some sensible comments with respect to the procedure adopted by governments in the past -and this does not apply to any particular party, it affects both the two old parties-in the matter of announcing legislation in the Speech from the Throne and introducing it subsequently into the House. So that the criticism of the right hon. leader of the opposition falls to the ground in that particular respect. If the present government had been the only sinner in the matter complained of, my right hon. friend's criticism might have had some weight and effect. In view of the actual facts it has no weight whatever. The right hon. gentleman has failed to recognize the fact that in almost every particular the promises contained in the Speech from the Throne have been implemented by legislation. Some of that legislation has met the fate that legislation of a similar character encountered in former days in the other chamber. As to that I have nothing to say.
To what legislation does my hon. friend refer?

My right hon. friend goes to the one question that we are not permitted to discuss, the one matter I have laboured harder to bring to a successful issue-I say it with all sincerity-than any other with which I have had to deal. If I am permitted to discuss it, I will say that having laboured zealously for at least ten years to bring about its settlement in the interests of the province which I represent, I see a shadow arising that will prevent that accomplishment perhaps for years to come. This government has not said that it has abandoned the hope of securing for the province of Alberta, its natural resources, not by any means. I, perhaps more than any other member of the administration, am desirous of bringing that question to a happy issue. The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Boutillier), who has just resumed his seat, says that he is anxious that national unity should prevail in Canada. May I say that even beyond my desire to secure for Alberta its natural resources I am anxious that we should have national unity in this Dominion. I am more desirous that nothing should happen to disturb national unity than I am of anything else. We who know something of the difficulties encountered in the past in connection with the question of provincial autonomy are not desirous of questions arising at any time that will tend to unfavourably influence and retard^ that national unity which should prevail in this country from one end to the other. speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
The last time this government was challenged in this House it was on the question of tthe grading of eggs, and the motion was moved by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). I do not know exactly what happened, but something seemed to backfire on that occasion, and1 my hon. friend from South Wellington did not seem to secure the support from his own side that he wanted. Now my hon. friends are taking up another problem, which is more momentous but entirely different. The amendment today is a challenge to the government on the ground that they have not carried out their sesssional programme as set out in the Speech from the Throne. That should be very easy of verification or refutation. We have the record and it is very easy to ascertain the facts. I have gone over it very hurriedly during the last hour. First, I refer to rural credits. In the Speech from the Throne the statement is made:
To this end a measure will be introduced offering wide facilities for rural credits.
The whole House was tumbling over itself to see who would be the first to propose a resolution relating to rural credits. One of my hon. friends opposite had a resolution on the order paper but withdrew it, and the government resolution was put through. That promise was carried out 100 per cent. That is tally number one.
Then the next matter to which I refer is the statement in the Speech from the Throne with respect to the tariff, which reads:
A tariff advisory board will accordingly be appointed forthwith.
Was that done? We hear a great deal about our not doing it quickly enough, but we did it as quickly as it could be done. Is the personnel of that board objected to by hon. members opposite? Is even the secretary objected to, as has been done this afternoon in the case of the secretary appointed to the Maritime Rights Commission? But in this case not even the secretary is objected to. That is 100 per cent again. Tally number two.
Then further:	_
Every effort will be made to further reduce expenditures. To aid in the reduction of expenditures in administration certain of the departments of the public service will be consolidated with others and government services more effectively co-ordinated.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Elliott) took over the department of Soldiers' Civil ReEstablishment. Is that an accomplishment?

That has been carried out. Tally number three. Further on:
In this connection a trade agreement entered into with the British West Indies, Bermuda, British Guiana and British Honduras will be submitted for your approval.
Has that been carried out? That has been done, no thanks to the Tories opposite from whom we heard nothing but yapping from start to finish. Hon. members talk of loyalty, patriotism and all the rest of it, but when it comes to doing anything practical there is nothing but talk. But there was not sufficient talk to stop the progress of this piece of legislation. I think that is score number four.
Number five.

Will somebody keep the tally? Then the next:
My government propose to submit provisions for the completion forthwith of the Hudson Bay railway.
Is that satisfactory to those who are most concerned in this enterprise? Do you hear one objection from any friend of the government in the west? The amount is $3,000,000. Is that not the exact sum my right hon. friend promised on one condition, namely, that that sum would be sufficient to complete the road to the bay, which he knew was impossible? We have placed it iD the estimates, it has gone through and it has not been challenged. And what has my right hon. friend to say, about it. Had we not talked so long in this House we might have got this put through earlier. I do not know of one single fair critic particularly friendly to the government who is not satisfied that we have done everything he anticipated with regard to that great enterprise. How much more could be spent? Would you want the whole estimated cost of $26,000,000 put' in the estimates? On one occasion we voted $350,000 and a great deal of dispute ensued, because we had not time to spend that amount, as it was late in the session. My right hon. friend cannot make any capital about the Hudson Bay vote up to the amount mentioned by him. There is no reservation by us that this will do the trick.
The next matter to which I refer is the statement in the Speech from the Throne that a royal commission will be appointed to inquire into the claims and the rights of the Maritime provinces. Has that been done?
Not yet.
Has any exception been taken to the personnel of the commission?
When will they start?

Some objection was taken to the secretary. One hon. member said he was a fine estimable gentleman, quite qualified in every respect but he had taken sides in the recent election, apparently against my hon. friend. Are you going to disqualify him because of that? Surely not. There we have another 100 per cent, and that is tally number six. I come now to the forbidden one.
Why did the hon. member leave out certain very important ones on the way?
I am taking them as they come.

The hon. member left
out two or three.

The right hon.
member will not have another opportunity to speak, but he can give the tip to some of his admirers to bring up what I miss. I have not finished yet. The next is a bill to provide for the transfer to the province of Alberta of its natural resources. Mr. Speaker, you have forbidden a discussion of that subject; but a good many hon. gentlemen have been eating the forbidden fruit if I know anything about the matter, and I wonder if you will let me get as near to it as they have. As the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) indicated, it takes two to make a bargain. There was a bargain put down in black and white, that this government concurred in, that the Alberta government concurred in. A resolution in regard to it was placed on the order paper. There it remained as was indicated by the recital of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) in this House a few weeks ago. We cannot force that on the Alberta government.
There must be two parties to a contract before it can be consummated. If one backs out the other cannot make the bargain with himself, unless there is concurrence and agreement in these matters. We could not have any June weddings without two parties to the contract. If one party defaults, the other cannot marry himself or herself. All they can do is to wait for a more favourable day, present their admonitions, and continue negotiations towards the desired end. Js that not what will be done? A more fortunate, a more acceptable time will no doubt come to the Alberta government, a time when it will be more opportune for them to accept the agreement than now. We do not know the minds of the members of that legislature. We know what was said to be the reason, but we do no* wan* tr repea* or to

Want o) Confidence Motion
elaborate it. The fact stands out that we can "resolute" from now to doomsday, but we cannot alone make a bargain. We are prepared to carry out the bargain on the terms mutually agreed upon by both sides. What more do hon. gentlemen want? This resolution is more absurd than the egg resolution of the other day. There was something to that resolution. It seems to be assumed by hon. gentlemen opposite that we can carry out this agreement ourselves, or in other words that one party can make a contract.
If my right hon. friend has anything to suggest as to what has been omitted from what the Minister of the Interior has indicated, it may be the amendment to the Elections Act. Was there any uproarious demand throughout the country for an amendment to the Elections Act? At the time that paragraph was inserted in the Speech from the Throne it was generally assumed by nine out of ten that we would need an election this summer. Was there the same apparent evidence of that during the last month? Was there the same necessity for it? Have we not had a long session? Is it not the natural thing, when you reach the June days, the hot days and the dog-days of summer, to eliminate anything that is least pressing that has been referred to in the House? Will there be any great alarm or anxiety or indignation throughout the country if this one item is not carried out? We can carry it out yet if that is required, but I do not see any evidence of any pressing need for it.
Let us consider some of the things that do not appear in the Speech from the Throne, but that nevertheless were forthcoming. Let us suppose that there is a balance on the wrong side with regard to the return of the natural resources. Something happened through no fault of ours. What about the introduction of the penny postage, mentioned for the first time by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) in his excellent budget speech? This is an old Liberal policy introduced in Sir Wilfrid Laurier's time by a former Postmaster 'General, Hon. Mr. Mulock. I know when the Tories came into power they raised it to three cents, a war tax if you like; but along with many other taxes we have removed this one cent war tax on letters and restored penny postage. subtopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
This bill has been before
the committee for some days, and to-day it was passed by just one-quarter of the members of the committee. It is a bill to incorporate a company to construct a railway from a point on the Canadian National railway into the Red Lake district. That territory is naturally Canadian National territory. If a railway were needed into that part of the country, the Canadian National naturally would be the company to construct it. In the past we have made many mistakes in railway construction in Canada. On account of the haphazard granting of charters for railways such as this, we find ourselves in the railway debacle which we are facing at the present time. This is a foreign company. The railway is not called for by anybody living in the district. A mining camp has just been started there, and no requisition has come to us for a railway. We have landed ourselves in a railway debt which we shall not be able to pay for generations. Before the committee grant this charter we should seriously consider whether we desire to incorporate a foreign company to go into the centre of this country to construct a railway where it is not wanted or called for at the present time. I am an advocate of government ownership, and I believe that this proposition cannot fail to have a detrimental effect on our Canadian National Railways. The idea of the promoter is that this railway will extend up through northern Manitoba and into the Hudson bay district, and I am wondering whether hon. members who so strenuously opposed the Hudson bay grant this year will now be willing to incorporate a company with powers to go into that district, exploit our natural resources, and intensify our railway problem. I oppose the bill for these reasons, and hope the committee will reject it.

subtopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
I was in the committee room when this bill came up to-day, and to my mind this is an exploitation company to get a charter which may hereafter become valuable. Not only does the bill ask for power to construct 100 miles of railway into Red Lake, but it asks for further power to go as far as The Pas, many miles northwest, and eventually become a new transcontinental line paralleling our two transcontinental lines across this continent. The Deputy Minister of Railways was present at the committee to-day and in reply to me he said that the department had no objection to it; but on behalf of the National Railways, although only a humble member of this House, I object to this free chartering of companies that are mainly for the purpose

Red Lake Railway Company
of exploitation, especially when, as was stated to-day, those who are asking for the charter are residents of the United States.
I think the time has arrived when the Minister of Railways should say whether he is willing to assume the responsibility of creating companies that are practically schemes for exploitation. It develops to-day that this is really in opposition to a parallel railway into which we are putting $3,000,000 now and into which we shall have to put $16,000,000 or $20,000,000 later on. Not only does it parallel that road to The Pas, but eventually if it means anything its object is to be another transcontinental railway in this country. The trouble in Canada is this over-duplication in regard to railways, and we are continuing in the same course. What we want to do is to get rid of these duplications. If a mining territory must be served with railways we ought to keep that for the National Railway system in preference to encouraging the construction of new railways. I have put in and I will continue to put in my protest hereafter against any schemes for railway construction for which good reasons cannot be given.
There may be a gold field there-I hope there is-but if there is, it is contiguous to the Canadian National Railways and the best way to get to it- is by the Canadian National. If the people there want to get a road they ought to go to the Canadian National and ask them to serve them by a line from their main line to this new gold field. Again I protest against this continuation of indiscriminately chartering new railroads that are to be subjects hereafter of trouble and expense to the Canadian National or the Canadian Pacific, and that are mainly promoted by those who are called dealers in charters or schemes that will eventually be a tax upon the people of this country.

subtopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
In the territory that I
have the honour to represent we have a new mining area known as the Red lake mining area. This application for a new railroad company - came before the committee, where is was turned down without very much consideration. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) very kindly brought it up again in this House and had it resurrected and sent back to the committee. At the next sitting of the committee sufficient information in -connection with the railway was not forthcoming from the promoters, and it was sent back again until they could give us some further information and until the Canadian National and the government of Ontario could be heard' from. The Premier of Ontario has written a letter to one of the northern Ontario members of this House who is interested in that territory and he states that with certain modifications he has no objections to the bill. The Deputy Minister of Railways came before the committee and1 the department has no objection to the bill.
In reply to the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), I may say that we have to-day included in the bill a special clause providing that construction must be under way and $100,000 spent within the first year. If that is not done at -the end of next session then all rights become null and void. We have taken out of the bill as it appears before the committee to-day certain clauses which the province of Ontario objected to in regard to water powers. Therefore I think the bill meets every objection, with the exception of the objections of those who are against all private enterprise in this country.
As -regards the statement of an hon. member opposite that this is a foreign corporation, I do not know where he gets his information. While I do not know any of these gentlemen I see that clause one reads:
John H. Cassidy, Charles B. Hibbard and Frederick R. Brown all of the city of Montreal, and D'Arcy Scott, of the city of Ottawa, together with such other persons as may become shareholders of the company are incorporated under the name of the Red Lake and Northwestern Railway Company.
It is true that the gentlemen when asking for incorporation told the committee that they had Boston 'bankers behind them, but I do not think it is a crime for anyone starting a new enterprise in this country to have it backed by foreign capital. At least, if that is the case, I have not yet heard it so stated.
The hon. gentleman said there was no request from the people of that district to have this railway built. As the member represent-

Red Lake Railway Company
ing that part of the country I am in a position to refute that statement. The district iies principally in unorganized territory and there are not very many councils or boards of trade, but such town councils as there are, like Dryden, for instance, are certainly demanding this railway. That particular council passed a resolution favouring the granting of the charter and as the representative of the people in the district I stand here to-night and say that they do want to have the railway built into that country.

Notwithstanding all that the hon. member has said, I still require further information before I can give my sanction to this matter. This railway will run across a corner of Ontario and into northern Manitoba, and according to the promoters of the bill it is intended to go into the mining area in proximity to Hudson bay. I am surprised to see how little interest parliament takes in this proposition, which in my opinion is a most unreasonable one. Our decision on this bill to-night will be a decision between public and private ownership, and whether we consider the National railways worth saving or not, the fact remains that we are dividing the

country up into small sections under private corporations to an extent which has been unknown in the past. We know to what pass the country has been brought through enterprises of this sort, and I fear it will not be long before the government will have to take over an unprofitable concern if we pass this bill. In spite of everything the hon. member has said as to the personnel of this corporation, I would remind the committee that the evidence came out before the Railway committee that a company of Boston bankers was behind the scheme, and I do not think that we in Canada have any occasion yet to invite any foreign company to come and tell us what we need in the way of new railways.

I should like to know from the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) what is the policy the government intends to pursue in relation to the government ownership of railways. It has been said that the Canadian National Railways are not interested in the matter. I would point out that those railways now belong to the people of Canada and it is for parliament to say whether or not the Canadian National system is interested.
