We are immensely interested in this matter and before the bill passes the House will no doubt demand further information.

subtopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
I oppose very strongly
this grab bill. I attended three sessions of the Railway committee when this bill was being considered. The committee saw fit to turn down the preamble, rejecting the bill for many reasons, among which was the contention that it was not in the public interest to pass this bill, that it was not a work for the general advantage of Canada, and that a territory containing such immense wealth should not be handed over to a few selfseekers and private corporations to be exploited for their own purposes and benefit. The entire railway policy of this country is all wrong and always has been. Parliament appointed a railway commission in 1917 for the express purpose of recommending what

Red Lake Railway Company
course should be followed in regard to just such matters as we are considering this evening. That commission made, among others, this recommendation, that before any bill was adopted by parliament it should first of all be passed upon by the railway commission itself. In the service of the commission there are experts who, from the information to which they have access and from the knowledge they possess, are able to decide whether such a bill as this is in the public interest or not, or is a work for the general advantage of Canada.
The proposed railway passes through a district in New Ontario which contains untold wealth, of which neither the provincial nor the Dominion government know the full extent. I do not think that anyone could possibly consider this project one for the general advantage of Canada. The road lies almost entirely in the province of Ontario, but it has been made by this bit of paper an interprovincial undertaking in order to bring it within the jurisdiction of this parliament. On three occasions the Minister of Railways has *been asked by the Railway committee to outline the policy of the government in connection with this bill, and the House has a right to know. The other night the minister himself introduced a vote for the Hudson Bay railway. If this bill passes and the proposed line is constructed it will run parallel to the Hudson Bay railway, and will take business away from that road.
I submit that this matter should be allowed to stand over for another year. There is no particular reason why we should rush it as not one yard of railway will be built this year. The company will not build, I say, a mile of railway this year, for an examination of the facts shows that the concern behind this application is nothing but a paper company. If we examined the records we should be surprised to find how many paper companies have been given charters for thirty years by this legislature. We should go over the books and wipe such companies out. I know of one company which was given a charter in 1905 and whidh came to parliament year after year with request for an extension of time and got fourteen extensions. This sort of thing should be put an end to. The time has come when the people will rebel against the taxation which they are called upon to bear in connection with railways in this country. We have spent millions of dollars on the National railways, and whenever there is any rich territory which might be developed for the benefit of the country at large, Sir Henry Thornton is prepared to hand it over to private concerns. On the other hand, there is
apparently too great a readiness to build branch lines which lead nowhere and will never yield a cent of revenue to the country. If these branch lines were built on the free trade law of supply and demand there would be fewer lines and fewer deficits and millions less cost to the country. The whole railway policy, I repeat, is unsound, and the time has come for a show-down. Are we going to repeat the fatal mistake made in this country from 1890 to 1911 when everyone could get a charter for the mere asking here in this legislature? One of the reasons why New Ontario has been economically annexed to the United States is the fact that American capitalists have secured control of the water-powers in that part of the country. These water-powers are the key to industrial development, and if Sir Adam Beck had been given his way and the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway had been electrified there would be in that district to-day, not
60,000	but half a million of people, and there would be such a development as has never been witnessed anywhere in the world, as the result of publicly bwned development of water-powers and transportation.
This is a purely provincial railway. If the promoter of this bill are anxious to put it through they ought to go to Queen's Park, Toronto. It is not and never was a work for the general advantage of Canada. I would ask the hon. gentleman who has spbken in support of the measure, who are the Americans back of it? What has Mr. Backus to do with this bill? He wrote to the Railway committee a letter in which he made the statement that he was prepared to build the road himself. Well, we all know that he is an American millionaire who waited upon the Ontario legislature in the days of the Drury-Raney farmer regime and was given a principality, a kingdom, an empire in itself of timber within New Ontario, all at the expense of the province. It is men of that type who are behind this undertaking. Mr. Backus is the silent partner who is ready to take the road over when we pass it, for he knows this parliament will never stand, or the public, for what he got away with in Ontario.
I am very much surprised at the action of the Ontario government under the premiership of Mr. Howard Ferguson. When Sir Adam Beck wanted the Whitney government to electrify the Temiskaming railway, private interests at that time opposed that policy, and the water-powers were handed over to private capital. I want to see the policy of protection adopted for this new part of Ontario. Are we going to repeat the mistakes we made in old Ontario; are we going to see the great corp'orations of
lied Lake Railway Company

New York, Boston, Toledo and Buffalo in control of the vast natural resources of that region? No I say the time has come to call a halt here and now and lay this bill over until we have the results of the survey parties which are now going over this new district. No one knows the wealth of the country to be served by this railway. There is no demand for this legislation. The territory should belong to the sc-called public ownership Canadian National Railways who support private grabs all the time. I am not surprised at the stand taken by the Premier of Ontario. He has always been on that side, and therefore it is quite natural that he should support this bill, but in doing so I believe he is making the same mistake in New Ontario that has been made in the older parts of the province. He fails to realize the possibilities of this newer New Ontario, as he failed to protect the 1914 New Ontario.
I am prepared, Mr. Chairman, to move by way of amendment that it is not in the public interest that this bill should be passed. Nobody knows who or what is behind this proposed charter. If you give to the promoters the powers they ask for under section 7 you will be giving them the individual key to that great district for ever, which is a kingdom in itself. It is purely a provincial railway, and instead of seeking a charter here the promoters should have taken a leaf out of the book of their great American millionaire leader Backus. He went to Queen's Park for his millionaire fake charters, and when he could get nothing more there, of course, he decided to invade the federal arena here. Not by the wildest stretch of the imagination can this bill be said to be a work for the general advantage of Canada. We are in effect being asked to grant a charter over the head of the Ontario legislature, over the head of the Canadian National and the railway commission. Who are the promoters of this bill? I know only one gentleman, Mr. D'Arcy Scott, whose address is the city of Ottawa. Before any more charters of this character are granted they should be reported on by the railway commission to the House. What is the railway commission for but to check up bills of this kind? I was glad to see the member for South York (Mr. Maclean) in the Railway committee this morning take a strong stand against the passing of this bill. I was there three days and missed him and his support. I am sorry a better hearing could not be had before the committee this morning, but no doubt the other members having already considered the bill two or three times had made up their minds with respect to it.

I am utterly opposed to the principle of this bill, Mr. Chairman. We should preserve this rich territory for the people of Ontario and the people of Canada, not deliver it over to these American millionaires whose names appear in clause 2 of the bill, Mr. Backus and his friends, who already have a kingdom up there in New Ontario. New Ontario to-day is owned very largely by American capitalists. The mining development of that country has been retarded owing to the lack of protection, which apparently some Conservatives rvould put on the scrap heap to-day for a few friends. The Conservative party in this honourable House is supposed to be a protectionist party. The most shining example we have to-day of the benefits of that policy is the hydro-electric movement in Ontario. The Hydro fought the battle of the masses against the classes, and saved and redeemed the water powers of Ontario without any help from Hon. Howard Ferguson, for the people of the province forever. Sir Adam Beck and myself, head and president of the hydro municipalities and as his first lieutenant respectively, often had to fight against the whole Ontario government and cabinet. We stood by our principles through thick and thin, in fair weather and bad.'
This .bill was considered a month ago in the Railway committee, and the application was refused. The committee then reported to the House, and the chairman of the committee moved concurrence in the report, which which was adopted by the House. But about two weeks later, a motion was made in the House to recommit the bill to the committee for further consideration. What happened between the first consideration and the second consideration of this bill by the committee I do not know', but the American interests got busy and in the first place I would say that I think it was a breach of the rules of the House to recommit the bill, and an abuse of the privileges of the House to send the bill back again. Secondly, I would point out that I have had three bills in the public interest on the order paper since January 12 on railway matters, one placed there on the 8th of January and one on the 12th, and they have never been called in this House except on one occasion at eleven-thirty at night, when I was not present and no one had any notice that the bill would be called. I contend, Mr. Speaker, that those bills have just as much right to. be heard before the standing committee on Railways as this favourite grab bill of private interests. This bill was recommitted to the committee, and the committee held two sittings, one last

Want o] Confidence Motion
Wednesday and another on Thursday, but the members did not get the notices in time and I moved that the bill be laid over for consideration until this morning. There was no letter written by the Premier of Ontario addressed to the committee, but there was a letter addressed to the gentleman who introduced the bill.
But what we have to consider, Mr. Chairman, is the public interest. That must be paramount in this House. Section 12 of this bill shows what this company is seeking. It provides:
The company may acquire (but not by expropriation) or lease and operate water-powers along the line of its railway or in the vicinity thereof and construct, maintain and improve dykes, piers, and flumes and all other works required for the development of such water-powers as well as for producing electricity or other power.
This bill is 95 per cent a power proposition. If you will read section 7 in conjunction with section 12, you will see what is behind this bill. Section 7 provides:
The company may lay out, construct and operate by means of steam, electricity, or other motive power a railway or tramway, from a point at, or near the village of Quibell in the township of Wabigoon, in the province of Ontario, thence in a northerly direction by the most feasible and advantageous route to a point at or near Red Lake a distance of about one hundred miles, then in a generally northerly and westerly direction to a point on the Hudson Bay division of the Canadian National railway at or east of Le Pas, in the province of Manitoba.
I contend, Mr. Chairman, that these sections are ultra vires of this parliament. Why? Because the government of the province of Ontario has seen fit to appoint a hydroelectric power commission having jurisdiction over all the water-powers of the province, including this territory, and I contend that it is outside of the power of this parliament to pass these provisions. Under the decision of the Privy Council the province has jurisdiction over all the water-ipowers that are entirely within the province for regulation and control purposes.
Not by any stretch of the imagination can this tramway of a few miles be said to be a work for the general advantage of Canada. The Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario was never consulted, and I say should never stand for any more of this kind of thing, and the people are going to protest, not only in the law courts, but through the ballot boxes. The older sections of New Ontario were so badly treated by the National railways that the province of Ontario had to build its own Temiskaming and Ontario railway without any federal subsidies, while
similar provincial railways built in Manitoba got millions in subsidies. I wish to protest, on behalf of the people of 9 p.m. Ontario, against the shabby treatment they have received. If necessary, this bill will be taken into the law courts to prevent the abuses it proposes. I protest against the bill passing, as I believe it is not in the public interest.

When you left the
chair, Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock, I was on the point of drawing attention to a certain snap verdict that our Conservative friends scored on the government in committee of the Whole about two or three months ago when the estimates of the Minister of Customs (Mr. Boivin) were before the committee. It was thought at that time by our Conservative friends that it would go abroad that the government was defeated by a majority of thirty odd, and that there would be a great sensation throughout the land, that a crisis would be precipitated, and that probably the government would be shaken out of the treasury benches. Well, Mr. Speaker, it did not work, you may have noticed. It fell on the public mind as flat as the proverbial pancake. They knew it was just a stunt, or. as described by my colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), it was just a matter of playing hide and seek. That is all it was-hide and seek politics. I must compliment them to-night on the more businesslike and manly way in which they are challenging the right of this government to govern. The hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Davis) has brought down an amendment. True, he forgot to notify us in the usual way, but that is a trifle in these days, I presume. It is the custom of two boxers when they first meet in the ring to shake hands, no matter how much they may want to kill each other. My hon. friends across the way forgot to shake hands by not giving

Want of Confidence Motion
us the usual notice that they were going to strike, but we will forgive them that trifle. I cannot help contrasting their attitude today, however, with the manly deportment and behaviour of the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) who gave me notice several days before that he was bringing down his famous egg amendment and challenging the government. Possibly one was only meant for the yolk, while this was meant for real blood.
I would like to inquire for a few moments what this amendment really does mean. If the contention of the right hon. leader of the opposition holds good, that is, that if we are defeated on this vote and ask for a dissolution and it is refused, we resign, then it will mean that the government of the country will go over into the hands of the Conservative party led by the lead'er of the opposition.
Hear, hear.

I am glad my hon.
friends see it that way, because that is the way I see it. Furthermore, it might dispel some of the illusions that some people have that some other leader might come to the front on the opposition side, for it is said that others have aspirations in that direction. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, there is no danger of the supremacy of the right hon. leader of the opposition being challenged in this respect by anyone. He will have a lot of good material over there out of which to make a cabinet, so let us be as cheerful as possible under the circumstances. There is no one he will choose quicker than his colleague who site to his right, the hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Rogers), a gentleman of well known cabinet material. Like myself and others, he has been in provincial political life' for many years before coming to Ottawa, and is recognized as having left his mark on the political life of Manitoba. I hope in my humble way that I too have left my mark on the provincial life of Saskatchewan. So I do not think the right hon. leader of the opposition will have any lack of material out of which to form a cabinet. It is therefore a fair fight and no favours, and may the best man and the best cause win.
There are far worse prospects than an election, Mr. Speaker. I could ask nothing better than to have a round out of our old traditional Tory friends, but I do not care much for the thought of spending a few thousand dollars in an election campaign in two successive years. I remember back in 1917, again in 1919, and again in 1921, I fought three successive elections, each two

years apart. There is not much money in that, Mr. Speaker, and from that angle I do not think much of the prospect of an election, but from the point of view of results I fear it not.
What would the carrying of this amendment mean in addition to turning the government of this country over into the hands of the Conservatives, led by the right hon. leader of the opposition? It is far better to' look this issue straight in the face and take plenty of time to consider it, than to vote upon it in haste and repent at leisure. Consequently I am not going to be in a hurry. Now I want what this step will mean to percolate into the minds of hon. gentlemen, especially those from the smaller provinces. There are two or three questions which have an important bearing upon it. There is no question but that the tariff is one of the questions. Nearly all our time during this session has been spent in discussing the tariff, and the election campaign to a large extent was fought on that issue. The government have followed up their election promises by making substantial reductions in the tariff not only on automobiles but pasteurizing plants in connection with our dairy industry, milking machines identified with the same industry, and many other articles that I could mention. There is no doubt that the right hon. leader of the opposition-and I say he did it manfully, openly and avowedly-challenged the issue of protection as against our policy of lower tariffs and wider markets. Consequently every hon. gentleman who deliberately throws the government of this country into Conservative hands and into the hands of the right hon. leader of the opposition is voting for a higher tariff and more taxation. There is no doubt about that. If it does not mean that then it does not mean anything at all. What is more, those who placed my right hon. friend in his present position and gave him a large number of seats in Ontario will have won their point. My hon. friends can rest assured of that. And so I say that every man who casts his ' vote for this amendment will be voting for a higher tariff. Had the Conservative party been in power do you think we should have got the present reduction in duties on motor cars? No, Sir, not at all. We may as well look the issue squarely in the face. We are going to have it settled and nobody will be allowed to wriggle out.
There is another very important question that has been before the House. It is one that has been before the country for twenty-five years, and that is the right of the farmers, particularly those in the west, to mar-

ket their own grain, in their own way, and through their own channels. I was identified with the fight for that long before I became known in any other capacity. We were forced into the contest by the exigencies of the situation. We had to do it, it was a fight for our lives, and this fight has been going on ever since. Every time the matter came before parliament, and there happened to be a Liberal government in power, we always got some redress in the direction desired ; we always made progress. I impress that upon hon. gentlemen.

Are you the member of this House whose name appears in Hansard of last year as voting against the amendment to the Canada Grain Act which is known this session as Bill No. 8?

It was the motion for the third reading of the bill and I voted for it. Had the wishes of my hon. friend and those.associated with him prevailed the whole bill would have been defeated. Mr, MOTHERWELL: We will do justice. My hon. friend need not perspire about it. When the House understand that the leader of the Conservative party in Alberta is counsel for one who was making the inquiry, he will understand more about it. Mr. MoGillivray

is counsel for the Live Stock Exchange in Calgary, and that is the interest my hon. friend is serving, rather than the United Livestock Growers, whether he knows it or not.

The hon. minister looks at
me and refers to me as though I were a substitute for the solicitor for that organization. Not until the present moment did I know who was the solicitor. I have never heard from him in connection with this matter. My interest was more along other lines than those suggested by the minister.

I am sorry the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) is not dn his seat, because I am going to pay a little attention to him. I think I take more fun out of this than anyone else on the other side. It always makes the right hon. gentleman look tired and feel tired when he is jollied a little bit. What will it be when the right hon. leader of the opposition becomes Prime Minister?

What about the

The report of that speech, which went through the whole of western Canada, reads:
Mr. Meighen stated that in the future it will be best for all that before the government takes a step in the direction of sending troops the will of the people should be known.
What does that mean? In the past we have taken the attitude that the will of parliament should be known, but this speech says distinctly that the people would be bound only by a submission of the question to them in a general election. Do not try to crawfish away from that. You might as well know what you will have to face if you are going to have an election. We may as well rehearse to-night-
Go on.

A short time before, I think in 1923, at the time of the trouble in the Dardanelles, my right hon. friend was ready to sally forth on the seven seas to fight anything in sight, without knowing what it was about or who was going to be fighting on our side. It was at that time that the right hon. gentleman made his "ready, aye, ready" speech without knowing whether there was going to be war with France or Italy or any other country. He was ready to go out and fight anything on the seven seas without knowing a thing about the matter. That was one extreme. The other extreme was just before the Bagot election-of course that was a coincidence

when he got down on his marrow-bones and was ready to do anything-to go to the people and have an election on the question. In other words he was going to turn this country into almost a civil war in order to determine whether it was to go into a foreign war or not. That is what will be meant, if words mean anything, by this parliament taking the desperate step of putting the affairs of this country into the hands of the leader of the opposition.
It means more than that. If we are to judge from our respective attitudes on the tariff, it means if the Conservatives are returned to power this time they will consolidate the financial and political influence in central Canada, a thing which has been such a bane of the outlying parts of Canada for the last many years. There is no question about that. I have no word to say against the older provinces in many respects. Ontario is my birthplace and I have a great respect for thartr province. But that is not the point. The Maritime provinces have been given some raw deals and the western provinces
right out to the Pacific have been neglected under Tory rule. That is what will happen again if this consolidation of wealth and political power becomes once more centralized in older Canada.
Look at the first step that was taken to consolidate the National railways. Everyone knows how dear to the hearts of the Maritime people was the old Intercolonial railway with its low freight rates. Who took it from them? The leader of the opposition and his party merged it with the Canadian National railway system, making no provision whatever for recognizing the tacit understanding of confederation that there would be such rates on the Intercolonial as would make it possible for them to deal with older Canada. Mr. Speaker, I trust in the few remarks I may make to-night I shall be more successful in keeping in order than I was yesterday. It seems to me there is favouritism shown in this matter. The resolution before us declares, in the language of the mover, that we should resolve, that this House because of failure to implement promises contained in the Speech from the Throne and for other causes has no longer confidence in the present government.
The question which immediately suggests itself is, what are these promises that have not been fulfilled? The hon. member who moved the resolution was kind enough to indicate one at least, namely, the failure of the government to carry out an agreement to restore to the province of Alberta its natural resources. So far as I know this was certainly not an issue at the general election. It undoubtedly was not an issue in the province of British Columbia, for I cannot recall having heard it mentioned once, either on the platform or in the press at that time. At all events, I received no mandate from my constituents in reference to the matter, and I imagine that most hon. members from that province are in the same position.
This strikes me as a somewhat narrow issue upon which to seek to defeat the government of the day. It has not been featured in the debates of this session. We have hardly heard of it except possibly from one or two men from the province concerned. It reminds me of a woman playing bridge, who persistently bid up hearts at every round until she got up to four hearts and then suddenly switched to five clubs. Why the switch? We have been fed the tariff for five years and especially during the last four months. That was the piece <de resistance of hon. gentlemen opposite. They fed it to us at every political meal ad libitum, not to say ad nauseam, and now suddenly they switch to clubs without notice, and apparently without design.

Similar motions on previous occasions have had hitched on to them other questions of such of character as utterly to preclude the consideration of the want of confidence aspect. For instance, there was a want of confidence vote in connection with the Australian treaty, and the importance of that treaty to the province from which I come altogether outweighed, in my opinion, any consideration of want of confidence.
I was elected as an Independent four years ago and again last year, although with the bitter opposition of what I may call the 14011-2884
Conservative machine. They were wont to declaim at great length, and with an almost total disregard of accuracy or of veracity, that my independent attitude in the previous four years had been entirely a camouflage and that I \ras decidedly and absolutely a supporter of the Mackenzie King government. Among some of the other things by which they sought to prove this charge, thinking it would hurt me in the election, was the statement that I had always in this House been opposed to any anti-Japanese legislation. The government, however, gave diplomatic reasons why in their opinion it was not wise to use a word said to be offensive and one which would hinder materially rather than assist negotiations with the Japanese government by which they hoped to achieve the same end, There was a full dress debate, and members from British British Columbia had a consultation among themselves as to whether they would accept the amendment of the government or not. The government said, "If you will accept this amendment we will put your resolution through unanimously", which was a considerable bait to us from that province who had never been able to put through a resolution so drastic. We had also to face this angle of the situation, that if we did not accept the government's amendment, they might reject the whole resolution. It was a matter for the critical consideration of those who had the interest of the subject at heart. Some

spite of this government, or partly both ways, perhaps it would be a good thing to continue the government in power so long as that prosperity appears to be at our door.

The Australian treaty, I think it can hardly be denied, has been a very material benefit-and its affects are only beginning to be felt-to the province of British Columbia. It has opened up the Australian market to our fish. I believe that we shall probably control in a very short time the whole Australian market, which is a big and an increasing market, and one of great value to the province of British Columbia. I was reading only yesterday that the fishing industry has gone up very much in the last year. The records are distinctly better than the previous year, and better than ever before in the history of the industry, and getting into the Australian market practically without competition is a matter of great and vital importance to us.
The same is true of the paper industry. Will my hon. friend kindly give us any precedent for his peculiar theory that because a prime minister has once held office, and has had a dissolution in the ordinary course, he cannot obtain another dissolution on account of a situation that arises in the House of Commons? There is no such precedent in British constitutional history.

On the contrary, Mr. Ramsay MacDonald received his dissolution because he had not sought a dissolution previously and obtained the will of the people; that is why. And what is more, the precedents have been reviewed at length with respect to that matter, and the rule laid down by constitutional authorities without end is that the sovereign will not within a reasonable time grant a second dissolution to one who has had a dissolution and sought the will of the electorate without obtaining a majority.

These things have happened, and now when we are in sight of the promised land we are told that we must be like Moses, die and not see it. I ask my friends from Alberta who belong to the Progressive party how they can go back to their constituents and tell .them they were precluded by the rules of the House of Commons from discussing this matter, and yet they must vote confidence in a government that has betrayed them most shamefully with respect to this transaction.
I did not intend to participate in this debate, but when I heard the observations of the Minister of Agriculture, when I heard the apologies of the Minister of the Interior, when I heard the blame that was heaped upon the government of the province of Alberta, and when I saw the attempt that was made to have it said that the government at Edmonton were responsible for the present situation I felt that although I did not belong to the party that had negotiated the terms of this agreement I must range myself on the side of the province. And having regard to the promise which I gave publicly and openly that I would support the agreement of January 9, 1926, I would be recreant to my own past history with respect to this matter, recreant to the trust reposed in me by the constituents that sent me here, if I did not rise in my place and voice a protest against the miserable subterfuge that prevents discussion of this matter and prevents the province of Alberta, perhaps for the next five or six years, from enjoying the right of administering its own natural resources as older provinces of this confederation do. That is the reason I have spoken, and I offer no apology for my action. If I have inadvertently disregarded in the slightest the ruling of the Chair this afternoon, I offer my most humble regrets, because I had no intention of doing so. My only object was to recite the facts I have mentioned, and say to my friends from Alberta that if to-night they vote confidence in this administration they must accept the responsibility of going back to their constituents and telling them
that the reason Alberta has not its resources is that they trusted the government of the day and were betrayed.
Hon. LUC1EN CANNON (Solicitor General) : My answer to the speech delivered by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) will be very short. The hon. member in the course of his remarks proclaimed that he respected the decision which the Chair gave this afternoon, that we should not discuss t'he question of the return of its natural resources to the province of Alberta. But every hon. member has no doubt remarked that most of the hon. gentleman's speech was directed to that question. I will bow to your decision, Mr. Speaker. I shall not follow the hon. member on the ground which he has chosen, but I will simply say, so far as the question of the natural resources of the province of Alberta are concerned, that this government will stand by the agreement entered into in 1905 and' will see that the rights of both the majority and the minority in that province are respected. If the hon. member who has just spoken is willing to have an election fought on the question whether the agreement of 1905 is to be nothing but a scrap of paper, and if he wishes to abandon the engagements which have been signed, engagements which have been consecrated by the governments which carried them out for the last twenty years, he is welcome to do so. But, on the other hand, we on the other side of the House are willing to meet him any time. We do not wish, Mr. Speaker, to have in Canada any religious struggles. We do not wish to revive in this country the dissensions which existed thirty and forty years ago; belonging as we do to the Liberal party, we are in favour of respecting the rights of minorities as well as the rights of majorities.

If the hon. member who interrupts wants to make a speech, let him make it; I am making one now. The amendment says that this government has not implemented its promises contained in the Speech from the Throne.
That is right-none of them.

When parliament met on the 7th of January what were the speeches delivered by members on the other side? They said that this government, in order to keep power, was delivering the whole of the country to the Progressives.
No; promising.

That is what they said. 1 remember in those days the board of strategy was wavering. It had not been established on as solid a basis as it is established now. Some of our friends, the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) for instance, would get up and say: We have nothing to do with the western element, the Progressives in this House. But the ex-Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) was not so hard to please. Fe said: If the Speech from the Throne does noc please the Progressive members, we will bring in one that may please them better.
We have worked for six months. We have brought in legislation, and mark my words Mr. Speaker, every piece of legislation brought in by this government has been adopted by the House of Commons. Not one of the government bills has been defeated; very few have been challenged, and to-day shall we, those who formed the majority while that legislation was being studied, turn round and say we have been wrong? Shall we, the Liberals on this side and the Progressives at the other end of the chamber, say that our labours for the last six months have been useless and should not be considered?
The right hon. gentleman, through the member who moved this amendment, says that we did not implement the Speech from the Throne. We have passed more progressive,

more liberal, more radical measures during this session than have been passed for many a year. The evidence of that is to be gathered from the Tory press of this country. If we wish to judge whether the legislation which was introduced was Liberal legislation, let us peruse for a minute the reports of the Canadian press directed, influenced and controlled in a large measure by hon. gentlemen who sit opposite to me. Let us think for one moment of what the press said when the budget was being discussed. We stood for radical changes in many ways. We carried them through.
And then changed them back again.

My right hon. friend interrupts. I have great respect for a leader of a party provided that he respects himself. I have always shown great respect for the right hon. gentleman; but if he wishes to interrupt me like a back-bencher does, I will answer him in the same way. I say that this amendment should not be carried because not only is it not straightforward, not only is it not fair, but, thirdly, it would not carry out its object.
What is the object of this amendment? It is censure of the government because the government did not implement the Speech from the Throne. Does anybody in this House outside of the dyed-in-the-wool Tories who surround the leader of the opposition believe for one moment that, were there a change in the government, the Speech from the Throne would be implemented? What measure wou'd the right hon. gentleman if he was Prime Minister to-morrow introduce into parliament to implement the Speech from the Throne? The amendment asks that this House should vote non-confidence in the government because it did not do enough to implement the Speech from the Throne. Can we expect the right hon. gentleman, or his neighbour the exMinister of Finance, or his other neighbour the ex-Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) to do anything further?
Suppose when the vote is taken the amende meat carries. What will happen? Two alternatives are possible. The first is that this government would resign and that the leader of the oppositon would be called upon to form a government. Let us consider this alternative as regards legislation implementing the Speech from the Throne. If to-morrow the right hon. gentleman became Prime Minster, this House would prorogue. Not another piece of legislation would pass. Any legislation which had been initiated and not completely adopted 14011-290
would be dropped. This parliament would cease to exist. Why so? The moment the right hon. gentleman accepted the position of Prime Minster he would cease to become a member of this House and would not be able to sit in this House. The moment he would choose his colleagues-land I hope he would choose our good friend the hon. member for West York-I am sorry to say he would disappear also. There would be in this House fifteen or sixteen empty seats. Does anybody think for one moment that we could carry on?
I hear that many appeals have been made to the Progressives by supposedly constitutional advocates carrying on one arm precedents dating back to Queen Anne and on the other memoirs telling us what Lord Beacons-field might have said on certain occasions. Our friends who are not learned in the law were told, I understand, that should the right hon. gentleman become Prime Minister we would have no election for two years. Has anybody with a sense of humour the gall to repeat that in this House. If the right hon. gentleman became Prime Minister to-morrow he would be forced, on account of himself and his colleagues not being able to sit in this House, to bring on an election. That is common sense. I do not know what Queen Anne said about the matter. Let us flake the other alternative, which is that the Prime Minister-

Our Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and I am proud of him The Prime Minister would ask for a dissolution. Now I heard a whole lot of constitutional law this afternoon; I have heard a lot more this evening, and I am not going to go into any details. As I said many months ago, common law is ordinary common sense, and constitutional law is common sense applied to public business. This government in January was told by a majority of the House to carry on the business of Canada, and we have done so. We have brought down legislation which has met with the approval of the majority of the House of Commons, and frequently these gallant knights who have spoken to-day did not have the courage to challenge a vote. If we were defeated on this amendment we should have the right to ask for a dissolution-and we shall have it. I heard the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) put the question, " Who ever heard of a prime minister asking twice in succession for a dissolution?"

Not asking but getting it.

What about Sir Wilfrid
Laurier, who was in power fifteen years and carried a number of elections? Was he not granted dissolution? Let us go further. Ramsay MacDonald formed a minority government, and when he was defeated in the House after having introduced his programme he asked His Majesty for a dissolution and he got it. And the crown in England is no different from the crown in Canada, notwithstanding what the hon. member for West Calgary may say to the contrary. I am not going to quote Gladstone; I am not going to quote Disraeli; I am not going to read any books-
It would be better for you if you did.
The hon, gentleman would like me to read books.
Hear, hear.

Well, I will not follow the hon. gentleman's example and drown my thoughts in a flood of words. This government has submitted to parliament a budget which has produced in the soul of the poor, of the weak and of the downtrodden a ray of hope, and we will not allow hon. gentlemen opposite who represent nothing but the great interests, nothing but selfish ends, to form a government before the electorate of Canada is called upon bo decide who shall govern the country. Let us have a vote, and if this government is sustained so much the better.
Oh, oh.
If the government is defeated, then we will go to the country. I fancy I hear someone opposite saying, so much the better if we are defeated.
Hear, hear.

I have no doubt a good many hon. gentlemen would be pleased to take our places, but that is a minor consideration. We are here to represent Canadian interests as a whole, and this is no time for a change of government.
Oh, oh.

Why do I say so? In a few months there is going to be an imperial conference and the League of Nations will meet; in a few months Canada will be called upon to express her views on international problems and on imperial relations.
War with Turkey?

Hon. gentlemen opposite have shown to-day an extraordinary sympathy for their leader (Mr. Meighen), and if they desire to have that sympathy maintained I would advise them not to talk Turkey. It will hurt the right hon. gentleman. He has taken such a stand, he has spoken on the same question in so many ways, that the less we speak about that subject the better for him. We are the representatives of the Canadian people, and we want as our spokesman, as our mouthpiece, a man whose ideals are Canadian and whose aspirations are the aspirations of the majority of the House.
